Hi! (Been a very long time!)

I am wondering if there is any prior art about using Lean to prove things about C programs.

To avoid the XY problem, I will describe why I want to know about this topic, but I'm not sure it's important to fully understand all the things I'm about to say:

  • There is a video game, Super Mario 64, which people are still actively studying.
  • In particular people investigate the A Button Challenge, which asks the question "how many times do you need to press A to complete the game?".
  • Interestingly, the current answer is that the upper bound is 13 A presses. But of course, the lower bound is 0 A presses; no one has proven that any particular A press is required to beat the game.
  • I am interested in exploring if I can make the lower bound nonzero, i.e. proving that SM64 requires at least one A press. This is much harder than improving the upper bound, since you'd have to somehow make an argument that no matter what you do, no matter what glitches may exist, you must press A.
  • Independently, a group of people once decompiled SM64 back to its original C code.
  • Synthesizing all this, I was thinking that if I could somehow prove facts about the decompiled C code, I could get towards a world where we could prove a lower bound for the A button challenge.
  • And thus I'll be asking a question about proving things about C programs in Lean.

I'll keep this open-ended: Is anyone aware of any prior art regarding proving facts about C programs in Lean?

My thought is that I will start on some sort of automated transpiler-y thing, which takes the C code and emits an IR, which can then be translated into a model in Lean, which can then perhaps be manipulated into proofs about said model.

Some intuition for why I think this isn't completely intractable:

  • I think you could prove basic things about certain C programs, like "this function calls that function unconditionally", or "this area of memory is written to only by this function", using static analysis/Clang.
  • I think those basic things could actually correspond to real-world truths about Super Mario 64, but in order to convince people that the proof is actually about SM64, it has to stem from an automated translation tool.

Any thoughts or prior art here? Thanks in advance :)
You could translate the C into unsafe Rust (using c2rust) and then use existing tools such as Aeneas

IMO this is a very big challenge with lots of hurdles to cross before one can reach something with bragging rights; could I suggest trying to prove things about routing in Pokemon (which also has decompilations) as a start? It's 2D, turn based, no physics, etc. which I think make the problem much easier to reason about.
Alternatively there may also be simpler things to try prove about the game, the "A button challenge" may be one of the more ambitious ones out there.
Also, no one knows whether pi is a regular number normal number, but surely we can prove that pi can't solve Pokemon? https://www.twitch.tv/winningsequence

Thanks for the pointers about c2rust and Aeneas, I wasn't aware of either of those so I will actively look into this.

(One such idea I had is proving that you need to press the Start button to start the game. And maybe we could go simpler still?)

Also, a couple nittier things about Pokemon that make it a little less attractive to me:

  • I don't know anything about it, but I have deep knowledge in SM64 already
  • Pokemon is written in assembly IIRC, and although it has been disassembled, it seems easier to reason about a game written in C maybe?

Regardless, I find it very unlikely that this process will lead to anything shaped like a strict bound or an improved upper bound. This is very NP-shaped, where the witness is sufficient for an upper bound improvement, and a complicated metaproof would be required for an improved lower bound.

Whilst it's interesting to talk about formally verifying claims about C code, I think that formally verifying that you need at least one A press to beat SM64 is surely completely unfeasible right now. Even disregarding things like the BLJ glitch which can send Mario through all kinds of barriers, there are other weird glitches which you're presumably well aware of (that guy a few years ago randomly upwarping in TTC on a live stream and nobody being able to reproduce for example (edit: found it)). Before you even start on this I think you'd need to have a concrete plan for some kind of invariant which you want to prove is preserved and given the amount of bugs in the game this seems like a really tall order. You can't prove by brute force that the invariant is preserved because surely there are going to be easily way more than 10^30 game states, and anyway can one really hope to prove that there's no arbitrary code execution bug which doesn't involve pressing A? A lot of these early N64 games have such glitches. Thinking about this problem and contrasting it with what people can currently actually do regarding proving things about C code (even proving trivial things about state after loops seems to be difficult) makes me think that this is science fiction right now. The complex N64 controller simply gives you too many inputs. Are you sure you don't want to start with SMB?
I would also add that C code is not enough, hardware also matters. And there's no formal model of Nintendo 64 hardware as far as I know.
And even that might be not enough, because you might be able to wiggle the cartridge a bit and win. Like it triggers a secret level select in some games: http://youtube.com/watch?v=ZZs2HUW9tDA.

Oh I think that the console wiggling stuff is out of scope for this. My objections are just about making any kind of formal statements about the code base when we know that BLJ and other glitches are able to write essentially random values (and certainly values which the code doesn't expect) to certain memory addresses. I am old enough to remember BLJ being discovered! That was somehow the beginning of this adventure but I think it also makes formal verification incredibly difficult.

Kevin Buzzard said:

The complex N64 controller simply gives you too many inputs. Are you sure you don't want to start with SMB?

I second this suggestion, even SMB1 is a highly nontrivial problem. The recent discovery of Arbitrary Code Execution in SMB1 shows that there is still things to be discovered in this game. Note that we still are not sure if ACE exists in SM64.

And to reiterate @suhr's point about hardware, this example shows how important it is to have a rock-solid formal model of the hardware. The SMB1 ACE uses subtle hardware exploits that don't exist in most emulators. So you need to test your model extensively to make sure it's faithful, for example it should pass 100th Coin's Accuracy Coin test.

Now assuming that we are given such a hardware model, my first question would be: "Can we put a lower bound for the number of frames to beat 1-1?" For years, the world record has been the 370 framerule, and it's quite likely that this is the best possible time. In principle, there are 8 buttons = 256 possible inputs on any frame, so brute-forcing 2563≈16256^3 \approx 162563≈16 million inputs proves that it is not possible to beat 1-1 in under 3 frames. Improving this bound would require novel methods.

Jack McCarthy said:

Improving this bound would require novel methods.

I think it shouldn't be difficult to prove you have to hold right a lot to finish the level, which would probably give you a lower bound close the true bound. (+ account for pipes and such)
So while glitches such as ACE are a problem, the exponential number of inputs doesn't seem like a huge problem (at least in SMB1 which is very linear).

The question is, can Lean imagine a bus?

Going from a memory overwrite bug to an exploit that optimizes some quantity sounds like the kind of exploit development task that AI is now good at. Maybe you could persuade an AI company to work on reducing the upper bound (possibly to 0) as a demonstration of the cybersecurity capabilities of their next model (using binaries with an ultra-accurate emulator, not a decompiled approximation)?

Some years ago (like 2018ish), DARPA gave some research grants for researching ways to identify worst case.inputs to programs so they could be used as attacks. In other words, if you knew algorithmically something about the system you were trying to attack, you could craft inputs in a way that would cause the memory or time of the system to blow up.

I vaguely remember some ideas about analyzing the possible execution paths in the program and then using a constraint solver to find inputs that would cause a particular branch to be reached

This is still a long way off from a video game though... Also, are the maps or levels part of the C code or separate data files? Wouldn't the feasibility depend as much on the maps as the game engine itself?

This is a common technique in the field (see e.g. angr), but usually done for small functions and as you mentioned it's not feasible for an entire game.

FWIW much like machine learning has been applied to video games, techniques for finding program inputs have also been demonstrated on games, see the cool image at the top of this fuzzing paper for example.

Thanks everyone for the thoughtful responses here. There is a lot to respond to, so I'll do my best, but I might miss some things.

that guy a few years ago randomly upwarping in TTC on a live stream and nobody being able to reproduce

I've actually done a lot of research into this specific upwarp, and I have concluded with medium-high confidence that it was a hardware issue with dupdome's console. I wrote this document about a similar incident that occurred to the same person's same console. Of course, I don't have 100% certainty of this conclusion, and agree that this does mean that my goal is out of reach without certain assumptions.

I think the assumptions are the interesting part because they have a few properties:

  • If the proof is upfront about its assumptions, everyone is on the same page and can decide whether to accept or deny the proof in their own mind.
  • The proof should be structured in a way where assumptions can be iteratively reduced through additional work. (I have some concrete thoughts on how to do this.)

can one really hope to prove that there's no arbitrary code execution bug which doesn't involve pressing A?

I agree that ACE is an important factor here. In particular I think that a core assumption of the 'proof' I'll be shooting for is that ACE is assumed nonexistent. I think this is an interesting, nontrivial assumption to make, because I claim that ACE is actually a well-defined class of bugs: if ACE exists, then we cannot trust the symbolic intent of the code (because it can be overwritten!). But if it is assumed not to exist, we actually can trust the symbolic intent of the code, and then the proof reduces roughly to:

  • Do you accept that the symbols used in the proof are actually the same symbols when we colloquially talk about concepts in SM64?
  • Is the proof valid? (i.e., we have to write the proof, which is hard!)
    and I think both of these things are separate and interesting.

even proving trivial things about state after loops seems to be difficult

This makes me concerned and I didn't know about this. I will need to look into this. Any pointers to writings about this topic would be great!

And there's no formal model of Nintendo 64 hardware as far as I know.

Sort of. There's CEN64, a cycle-accurate N64 emulator. This codebase could be considered such a model.
However, I agree directionally with your claims that (1) hardware matters, and (2) it makes the proof even loftier of a goal to include hardware. I think this goes back to my assumptions point above; v0 of the proof should not worry about hardware, but a future vN might.

Oh I think that the console wiggling stuff is out of scope for this

I completely agree.

discussion of SMB, etc

I want to take a step back and acknowledge that although SM64 is much more complex than SMB with respect to its inputs and state, I think they aren't that far apart for the types of questions I'm interested in answering. The fact that SM64 is fully decompiled and its code well-documented means we can make statements about symbols; this is true of both SM64 and SMB.
Also, I'll point out that the types of things discussed earlier in this thread, namely "a minimum number of frames needed to beat 1-1", seem meaningfully different, and actually much harder, than the logical qusetion of "is the A button required for 120 stars".

I think I failed to make this clear in my original post, so I actually will now attempt to show why I think this is tractable. The thing I think is within reach is proving that Wing Mario over the Rainbow cannot be beaten in 0 A presses. In this level, you need to collect 8 red coins. One of the red coins is at the bottom of the level. Another is at the top. The current strategy requires 2 A presses, both times used to shoot out of a cannon.

So I think the very very rough shape of the proof goes something like this:

  • We can maybe prove some facts about how level loading works, i.e. the fact that only certain platforms and objects are initialized, and some facts about how Mario's state is initialized.
  • Using those facts, combined with some facts about WMotR's specifics, we can begin the proof.
  • We can maybe prove that to make the star appear, you need to collect the 8 red coins at specific coordinates.
  • If so, we can definitely prove that we need to collect those 2 specific coins, i.e. the one at the bottom and the one at the top.
  • We can maybe prove -- this is the super hard part -- some facts about all the code in the entire codebase that modifies Mario's y-value, and do casework to prove that each one is not achievable (owing primarily to the fact that WMotR has very little to work with; we can rule out entire code paths, and for others we can make energy conservation arguments).

Does this make a bit more sense? I'm saying that this proof will reside in symbol-land, about "real life concepts" in WMotR.

I think the SMB equivalent of this might be e.g. proving that you need to press A once to beat 1-1. (I don't know a lot about SMB so actually this might not be true? But the argument would go like: You need to touch the pole to beat the level; and the only code that increases Mario's y-value is code inextricably attached to the A button.)

Maybe you could persuade an AI company to work on reducing the upper bound (possibly to 0)

This is a long, long ways off IMO. Complexity-theoretically, there is a true value for the SM64 A Button Challenge upper bound, and in my heart I believe that value to be 12. Of course it could be lower, and if ACE could be achieved then it could be as low as 0 (assuming you don't need to press A to achieve ACE!), but anyway my point is that I don't think an AI lab is very interested in this because the input state space is absolutely massive, and a much better way to explore the output state space is by doing reasoning about "real-world concepts" in the game (i.e. objects and glitches).
In particular I think fuzzing is just out of the realm of likelihood for saving A presses, as there is just too much going on state-wise and exploring any interesting part of it would require genuine intuition about the game's pieces and logic.
I don't think AI models have a particularly good world-model about video games due to their being a very visual medium, so I don't know if this is something the labs would be that interested in. (They'd get massive bragging rights and make big news if they did save an A press, though!)

TL;DR:

  • I think the proof will have two major components: (1) proving that it is a meaningful proof that actually corresponds to the real game, and (2) the proof itself making interesting arguments about the game's code, under some (perhaps reducible-over-time) assumptions.
  • I think this is more tractable than it sounds because my initial goal seems intuitively obvious to me. Of all the A presses that won't be saved, this is the won'test.
  • Rocq and Clight (but not VST) seem very applicable here, and I am going to start pursuing that route (even though I'd be a bit sad to use Rocq instead of Lean... wink wink!).

AI models have been good at processing images for a long time, I don't think being a visual medium should be a problem there. And effectively the task for an AI model reducing A presses would be to search the binary of the game to find as many glitches as possible and then try to program the weird machine constructed entirely out of glitches, which is the sort of thing they do when writing exploits. Unlike exploits for currently maintained and used software, where there are questions of responsible disclosure, the AI companies would be able to release any such exploits found in an old game immediately.

I don't think working with a decompiled C version would ever be a good approach for proving things about a specific game binary. There are too many things in C that are undefined or unspecified, and it's exactly those areas that are most ripe for finding exploits (where the exploit or proof of its absence needs to care about exactly how the actual hardware behaves with the actual instructions in the binary, not about the wider range of possible behaviour permitted for C). Writing a formal model of the hardware is surely a very large job, but it seems more relevant to this problem than a formal model of C.

To close the loop here, I have made some very small initial progress on this very ambitious project by starting with the aforementioned Clight/clightgen/Rocq strategy kindly referenced by @Snir Broshi above. (Thanks!)

I'm honestly feeling really good about it. (I'm trying not to let the LLM psychosis set in ;) ). I seem to have stronger-than-average priors that this is easier-than-impossible, so I'm giving it a go.

Feel free to follow along here, although I want to be very clear that this initial work is classic proofslop generated by an LLM (akin to merely-true). The repo is here: https://github.com/matt-kempster/sm64-wmotr-abc-proof

It's very possible I run into a hard blocker very soon, but hey, you never know!

Thanks again for all the pointers in this thread!!
(@Snir Broshi was the sad react intentional? Didn't mean to offend if so!)

Intentional but not because you offended me, everything is good!
I'm just slightly disappointed that this thread lead to "proofslop" as you called it.

Ah, I can see how that might not be the best outcome for this community, sorry :(

Fundamentally I would of course like to write a good proof here, and I'm not saying the door is closed for that to happen, but I think two other things too:

  • I really want to know if this fact about SM64 is true, at the expense of many things
  • I think this 'proofslop' thing is kind of known to happen with CompCert style proofs? Even before LLMs? I don't have a source for this claim, but I've seen it when doing some cursory searching, and intuitively it makes some sense. If you're trying to prove that a program that powers an airplane doesn't crash, the proof of that is worth more than the beauty of the proof?

I'm not sure that you've really internalised how phenomenally difficult it is to prove theorems about even the simplest C code at this point in time, and I fear that if you're pouring money and tokens into this then it will be a complete waste of them. Before you start proving anything about SM64 why don't you write some C code which generates a random 1000000x1000000 maze with some exits and then puts a character randomly in it, which can move around in the maze using cursor keys, and then write some Lean code proving that either the object cannot get out of the maze, or that it can get out of the maze? That project is surely many orders of magnitude easier than what you propose doing.

Matt Kempster said:

If you're trying to prove that a program that powers an airplane doesn't crash, the proof of that is worth more than the beauty of the proof?

That implicitly assumes that if Lean says the proof is correct then it really is correct, which is false (even if it has no sorry).
I don't want to derail the discussion too much, but see Did you prove it?, and #Autoformalization > Atlas (Meta) for example.

At the end of the day, even if you get a compiling proof, unless you can read and understand it (at least the definitions and statements) you will not be able to make any claims about whether the fact is actually true or not. So throwing tokens at the problem cannot lead to the outcome you want.

Kevin Buzzard said:

either the object cannot get out of the maze, or that it can get out of the maze?

is this supposed to be excluded middle?

For reference, LibSignal, the reference implementation of the Signal protocol, is about 5 million bytes of Rust code. Rust is already a very nice language to formalize since it makes strong guarantees about memory safety, plus it runs on modern hardware (which can be assumed trusted).

By contrast, the SM64 decomp is over 31 million bytes of C code. Much of that code has memory leaks and bugs. Some of the code utilizes undocumented behavior and hardcoded memory addresses that are specific to the N64 console in order to trigger hardware interrupts, IO reads, etc.

If #Signal Shot is considered a moonshot, then this is in a whole other galaxy.

At the end of the day, even if you get a compiling proof, unless you can read and understand it (at least the definitions and statements) you will not be able to make any claims about whether the fact is actually true or not. So throwing tokens at the problem cannot lead to the outcome you want.

I unconditionally agree, and it's top-of-mind for me. I'm taking great care to make sure this project is structured from the ground up in a way that reduces the chance I end up proving something other than what I want to prove. I'm building on top of CompCert/clightgen, which have done a lot of the heavy lifting around transpiling the C code to a prover language. And as the proof starts to slowly take shape, I'm going to be extremely careful about reading and understanding the definitions and assumptions (explicit or implicit) used.

I fear that if you're pouring money and tokens into this then it will be a complete waste of them

I completely acknowledge this and will be mindful. Your message has definitely updated me away from spending extra money on this. (I'm still fitting within my $20 claude/gpt plans, which I have for many other reasons than just this project.) So thanks!

why don't you write some C code which generates a random 1000000x1000000 maze with some exits and then puts a character randomly in it, which can move around in the maze using cursor keys, and then write some Lean code proving that either the object cannot get out of the maze, or that it can get out of the maze? That project is surely many orders of magnitude easier than what you propose doing.

(I'm going to first of all assume you didn't mean law of the excluded middle here, because that would be trivial.)
I'm actually quite confident this is harder than what I am proposing. I'm trying to prove an impossibility statement, but your example is a decision over a random instance. There's a few things here:

  • SM64 is a specific instance. It is not random. (It has PRNG, but it will not come into play for this proof; see below.) A random maze doesn't have any structure to exploit. SM64 was hand-crafted by humans, with a codebase that is readable in plain English. It does contain some structures similar-ish to a maze, but there's no maze in the thing I'm trying to prove.
  • Similarly to above, I'm not trying to decide whether we can or cannot escape the maze. I have a strong conjecture that you cannot escape one specific maze, and I am trying to prove it.
  • (My confidence about this bullet point is maybe 20-30%.) When proving an impossibility theorem, you can stub out substructures and make sound overapproximations of their behavior. seL4 needed to write what are effectively a billion tiny unit & integration tests; if I were trying to prove everything about SM64, I'd need to do the same, and it would be a gargantuan task. But since I can stub out subsystems, I don't need to prove full functional correctness, I just need to prove very specific facts.

the SM64 decomp is over 31 million bytes of C code

See above, I am not going to need to check all 31 million of those bytes. But I do appreciate the sense of scale, and could absolutely be wrong in my belief that overapproximations will be possible here.

Much of that code has memory leaks

SM64 does not have memory leaks. There is no malloc() nor free(). The entire state of the game is held in fixed memory pools.

Some of the code utilizes undocumented behavior

Not very much of it, and the code that does isn't that interesting. (Grep for AVOID_UB in the codebase.)

(I should probably disclaim that I was one of the members of the decompilation team for SM64, so I happen to know a lot about the codebase.)

(Sorry if this message sounds hostile -- I really really really don't want it to sound that way! I'm just providing my point of view in the form of counterarguments. I respect everyone here and don't want this to devolve!)

I probably should've been more generous about the term "memory leak". The following things definitely exist to a great extent in the codebase:

  • Stale pointers
  • Memory reuse
  • Union type-punning
  • Out-of-bounds reads and writes

But I'm facing those head-on. I intend to write proofs about them. I still think those proofs will be tractable.

Well, it sounds like you're aware of the risks and going to proceed anyways. I wish you the best of luck! It will certainly be impressive if you manage to produce a proof which isn't AI slop.

But I agree with Kevin's suggestion that you might want to start with a toy example first. Based on the maze idea, you write:

Similarly to above, I'm not trying to decide whether we can or cannot escape the maze. I have a strong conjecture that you cannot escape one specific maze, and I am trying to prove it.

In that case, make an impossible maze game! Try to prove that it's really impossible. If you do that, I'd be very curious to see the prototype.

It will certainly be impressive if you manage to produce a proof which isn't AI slop.

To be extra clear, I do not think this is going to happen. Unless something changes, the nitty-gritty of the proof is going to be slop. I'm sorry. But the, uh... "whole proof"(?) will not be slop. The sum total of the Rocq proof alongside its assumptions, definitions, and setup will not be slop, and will instead be understandable, etc.

make an impossible maze game! Try to prove that it's really impossible. If you do that, I'd be very curious to see the prototype.

Are you proposing that I write a game in C with a hardcoded maze and a start position, and prove that there is no path to the exit? That does not sound very hard to me (well, the 1000000 x 1000000 part is too hard, but I'll just do 100x100 or something instead. Super Mario 64's code and data fits within 4MB!). I might give it a try.

FWIW, I already have a very very simple, toy proof in the repo I linked above about a specific function in SM64, just to play around with the tooling. The function (from shadow.c) is:

  /**
   * Dim a shadow when its parent object is further from the ground.
   */
  u8 dim_shadow_with_distance(u8 solidity, f32 distFromFloor) {
      f32 ret;

      if (solidity < 121) {
          return solidity;
      } else if (distFromFloor <= 0.0) {
          return solidity;
      } else if (distFromFloor >= 600.0) {
          return 120;
      } else {
          ret = ((120 - solidity) * distFromFloor) / 600.0 + (f32) solidity;
          return ret;
      }
  }

and the theorem statement in Rocq is

Theorem dim_shadow_low_solidity_returns_solidity :
  forall ge m t m' vres i d,
    (* solidity is a genuine u8 ... *)
    Int.zero_ext 8 i = i ->
    (* ... and below the 121 dimming threshold. *)
    Int.lt i (Int.repr 121) = true ->
    eval_funcall function_entry2 ge m (Internal f_dim_shadow_with_distance)
      (Vint i :: d :: nil) t m' vres ->
    vres = Vint i /\ m' = m.

which says that if solidity < 121 then the function returns solidity.

I readily admit: This is not a very interesting proof. The function is pure, so none of the hard things that happen in entire codebases have happened yet. But I've technically proved something about SM64 now.
